body: Area codes in Japan increase as you move south; codes ending with 0 are often not regional.
Every Japanese region has a distinctive pole plate design on utility poles.
Pole reflector pads in Japan vary depending on the region.
Road diamond styles can help narrow down the Japanese prefecture you are in.
Most Japanese prefectures feature unique stickers on signposts for identification.
Many regions in Japan have unique guy wire designs on utility poles.
An orange arrow above the top pole plate can be found in the Chugoku region.
Orange and black bands wrapped around poles are common in Shikoku.
Poles in Kansai often have attachments with an approximate 120-degree angle.
Smaller 90-degree angled pole attachments are found in Shikoku.
Hokkaido's electrical poles often have plus-shaped bars or transformers mounted on two bars with no wooden plate.
Tohoku transformers feature square mounting with zigzag or straight bars and the Tohoku Electric Company logo.
Kanto transformers have two or three insulators mounted on wooden or round plates with T-shaped bars.
Hokuriku transformers have thin metal bars and small clamp-shaped insulators; Niigata uses Tohoku design.
Chubu transformers often have yellow paint and tap connectors, attached with triangular or thin metal brackets.
Kansai transformers have straight or zigzag bars mounted at the bottom of squares, with transformers on the sides.
Chugoku transformers have cross-shaped bars with triangle mounts and colored number stickers.
Shikoku transformers have cross-shaped bars with half-triangle mounts and hat-shaped insulators.
Kyushu transformers have straight bars with three insulators mounted opposite each other.
Okinawa transformers have T-shaped bars with transformers mounted on opposite pole sides.
Grey insulator-like blocks feeding wires are common in Chubu, Kansai, Chugoku, Shikoku, and rarely Hokkaido.
A pole top with four thicker bars and a circle is common in the Chubu region.
The Hokuriku region features tent-shaped pole tops with two filled sides.
Four thin, skinny bars characterize common pole tops in Chugoku.
Kanto pole tops often have a tuning fork shape with a long top bar and horizontal bars below.
In Chubu, tuning fork pole tops usually have a short top bar with horizontal bars below.
Kansai tuning fork pole tops feature a thin wire and horizontal bar beneath.
Hokkaido-specific infrastructural arrows show shoulder lines under snow, mostly yellow with rare regional variations.
Flat white bollards with separated orange reflectors are common in Kyushu and Yamaguchi.
On Shikoku, some bollards have a black stripe below the reflector and are attached to guardrails or walls.
Thick white bollards in Tohoku have octagonal reflectors with yellow stripes and can be found on highways.
Akita variations include two yellow stripes below octagonal reflectors on thick white bollards.
Toyama's extendable bollards have one octagonal reflector with a red stripe beneath.
Okayama bollards have an octagonal reflector with a red stripe and a sloped connection to the base.
Aomori bollards have two yellow stripes, one circular reflector, and are extendable.
Tohoku striped bollards have thin tops without reflectors, common especially in Akita.
Northern Chugoku features basic snow poles with thin extended or contracted tops.
Green guardrail bands are mostly in Oita and Miyazaki and found throughout Kyushu.
Yellow guardrails are typical in Yamaguchi Prefecture.
Chevron-like stickers are found on guardrails in Hokkaido, including orange, yellow, and green variations.
Red and yellow striped guardrail endings are common across Chugoku and rarely in Niigata.
Vertical traffic lights appear in Hokkaido and northwest coast; horizontal lights are found elsewhere.
Kagawa's black signs contain two yellow circles and various configurations.
Kerosene tanks, known as 'Claymores,' are common further north, especially in Hokkaido and mountainous areas.
Hot water, gas, and propane tanks, including cylindrical and tripod types, are frequent in northern regions and rural towns.
Snow prevention roads in northwest coastal prefectures spray warm water through pavement to clear snow.
Cycling routes in Ehime use white outer and blue inner lines, mostly coastal but sometimes inland.
Red-tiled roofs characterize Chugoku, especially in Hiroshima and Shimane prefectures.
Roofs transition from tiled in the south to flat/sloped with ladders in snowy northern or mountainous regions.
Okinawa is recognized by its white concrete buildings with flat roofs.
Cabbage is widespread in Hokkaido and northern prefectures, with smaller leaves found further south.
Green tea is grown mostly in hedged rows in Shizuoka and Kagoshima, with minor production in other prefectures.
Rice production occurs north of Tokyo, growing in water beds, with major production in Chubu, Kanto, Tohoku, and Hokkaido.
Japanese White Birch mainly grows in Chubu and Hokkaido; bark is mostly white, unlike Japanese Beech's grey spotted bark.
Bamboo grows more frequently in the south, decreasing gradually northward.
Chinese Silver Grass is abundant in Kyushu and parts of Niigata, Yamagata, and Akita, often recognizable by distinct vegetation.
Sugarcane is almost exclusively grown on southern Kyushu and Okinawa islands.
Hokkaido has very limited winter and snow coverage; most coverage is scattered in the southern half.
Japan is mountainous, with the Nobi and Kanto plains being notable flat regions useful for location identification.
Okinawa is identifiable by Shisa guardian lions and house plaques carrying unique characters.
Red soil agricultural fields are common on southern islands, particularly Miyakojima and Ishigaki in southern Okinawa.
Mount Fuji, Japan's tallest mountain, features a gradual incline and often snowy summit, visible from far away.
Tokyo has a unique manhole design with a five-petal flower pattern and multiple small circles.
Cyrillic script can be found on signs in Wakkanai and Nemuro in northern Hokkaido.
Date city in Hokkaido has artistically painted poles resembling birch trees.
Japan has diverse trekkers and tripod camera setups spanning many prefectures; further resources are recommended for details.
